description: We are a multidisciplinary engineering team building MOSAIC-9, a mission health intelligence and event-reconstruction platform for long-duration human spaceflight. Our system combines personal health baselines, temporal event analysis, explainable intelligence, incident replay and offline-first operations to help astronauts understand evolving health patterns. We welcome collaborators in aerospace science, biomedical research, AI, software engineering, data visualization and human factors.
summary:
MOSAIC-9 (Mission Health Event Reconstruction for Deep-Space Crews) is an explainable mission-health intelligence platform designed to help astronauts and mission teams understand evolving health and performance events during space missions.

Rather than simply displaying health indicators, MOSAIC-9 connects physiological, sleep, workload, exercise, and environmental context into a time-ordered evidence trail. Its key capabilities include individual crew health baselines, temporal relationship analysis, health incident reconstruction, a mission evidence graph, and a countermeasure scenario sandbox for exploring operational trade-offs.

The platform draws on NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) research and NASA Human Research Program resources to provide scientific context. Its demonstration uses clearly labelled synthetic crew telemetry and fictional crew profiles, not live astronaut medical records.

MOSAIC-9 aims to make mission-health information more understandable, traceable, and useful for human review, especially when communication and resources are constrained during deep-space exploration.
details:
MOSAIC-9 — Mission Health Event Reconstruction for Deep-Space Crews

1. What We Built

MOSAIC-9 is an explainable mission-health intelligence and event-reconstruction platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Long-duration space missions create interconnected health and operational challenges. Changes in sleep, workload, exercise, cardiovascular indicators, and environmental conditions may develop over time and interact with one another. Looking at individual measurements in isolation can make it difficult for a crew or mission-support team to understand how an incident developed.

MOSAIC-9 addresses this challenge by bringing mission-health observations, individual baselines, temporal relationships, and supporting evidence into one traceable operational workspace.

2. How It Works

The platform organizes mission information into a time-aware intelligence workflow:

Observe → Connect → Reconstruct → Explore → Review

  • Mission Command Center: Provides an overview of crew status, mission events, operational indicators, and emerging areas requiring attention.
  • Mission Health Intelligence Ledger: Organizes time-stamped observations and events into a traceable record.
  • Personal Crew Health Twin: Provides an individual reference context for understanding changes against a crew member's represented baseline.
  • Temporal Relationship Intelligence: Examines exploratory relationships between sleep, workload, exercise, and physiological indicators over time.
  • Health Incident Reconstruction: Reconstructs the sequence of observations surrounding a health-related event, showing what was observed, what was derived, what remains uncertain, and what evidence is missing.
  • Mission Evidence Graph: Connects observations, derived indicators, NASA research context, exploratory hypotheses, and missing evidence.
  • Countermeasure Scenario Sandbox: Compares alternative operational scenarios through model-based trade-offs, including recovery trajectory, operational continuity, and exercise preservation.
  • Offline Mission Operations: Supports local operation and queued ground-communication records when connectivity is interrupted, subject to the application's actual host and storage requirements.

3. What Makes MOSAIC-9 Different

MOSAIC-9 is designed around event reconstruction and evidence traceability rather than another conventional health dashboard.

It distinguishes direct observations from derived temporal associations, exploratory hypotheses, missing evidence, NASA research context, and synthetic simulation records.

This distinction matters: a system should not present a correlation as a proven cause, a simulated outcome as a medical recommendation, or missing telemetry as evidence that a crew member is healthy or unwell.

The platform makes uncertainty and data provenance visible so that crew members and mission-support personnel can review the available information instead of relying on an unexplained automated conclusion.

4. NASA Research and Evidence

MOSAIC-9 references NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and Human Research Program (HRP) resources to establish scientific context around spaceflight-related cardiovascular, sleep, workload, and other health risks.

These resources provide research context and evidence references. They are not presented as live astronaut telemetry or as direct clinical validation of MOSAIC-9.

The Inspiration4 OSDR research includes pre-flight and post-flight biological samples. Other referenced studies examine specific experimental models and biological processes. Their scope is preserved rather than treating all research measurements as interchangeable with real-time crew monitoring.

5. Demonstration Data and Scientific Integrity

The interactive demonstration uses four fictional crew profiles and synthetic mission telemetry. These records are deliberately labelled as synthetic.

The platform's temporal relationships are exploratory and based on small demonstration windows. They do not establish causation or clinical significance. Confidence indicators are heuristic measures of evidence alignment and completeness, not clinical probabilities.

Countermeasure scenarios are model-based operational comparisons, not medical prescriptions or autonomous treatment decisions. Mission personnel retain responsibility for interpreting evidence and following appropriate procedures.

6. Technology Stack

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, ECharts, and Lucide icons.
  • Backend: Laravel and PHP.
  • Intelligence service: Python and FastAPI, with NumPy, Pandas, and SciPy.
  • Database: SQLite with WAL mode.
  • Application capabilities: API-based service integration, interactive visualizations, local data handling, and connectivity-aware communication workflows.

7. Intended Impact

MOSAIC-9 aims to improve the interpretability and traceability of mission-health information. By reconstructing how events develop over time and clearly separating evidence from uncertainty, it can help make complex mission information easier for humans to review.

Our long-term vision is to support more informed crew-health discussions and operational planning for future lunar and deep-space missions.

MOSAIC-9 is a research and demonstration prototype. It is not a clinically validated medical device, an operational NASA system, or a flight-certified platform.
